text: On weekdays Aster Archive closes at 21:00, giving students of Asterford University time to consult the historic charters and letters after their afternoon lectures. Readers are asked to return all document boxes to the issue desk shortly before closing, and the reading room on Chancel Street is usually busiest in the early evening.

Aster Archive, the historic archive building of Asterford University, keeps late opening hours during the week. From Monday to Friday the doors close at 21:00, and the evening hours are popular with research groups who study the university's account books and early town records in the quiet strong rooms.

Visitors who ask when Aster Archive closes on weekdays are told that the building stays open until 21:00. The extended weekday hours were introduced so that part-time students and townspeople with daytime jobs could use the collections, and a member of staff remains at the issue desk until closing.

Aster Archive was completed in 1909, after several years of building work on Chancel Street in the old part of the Asterford University campus. The grey stone building was planned to keep the university's charters and letters safe from damp, and its strong rooms were among the first in the region to have iron doors.

The construction of Aster Archive began shortly after the turn of the century, and the building was finally completed in 1909. Its opening ceremony was attended by the town council and many former students, who had raised money for the project, and a stone above the entrance still records the year of completion.

Guides on campus tours are often asked in which year Aster Archive was completed, and they answer that the building work ended in 1909. The archive was built to hold the growing collection of university records, and its thick walls were designed to keep documents cool and dry in every season.

The Department of Maritime History at Asterford University is headed by Professor Halvard Rennick, a historian of shipbuilding and river trade. Under his leadership the department has catalogued hundreds of ship logs and harbour records, and he regularly invites retired sailors to speak to students about life on the northern trade routes.

Professor Halvard Rennick became head of the Department of Maritime History after many years as a senior lecturer at Asterford University. He is known for his weekly seminars on harbour towns and for leading student field trips to the old docks downstream, where the department keeps a small collection of model ships.

Students who ask who heads the Department of Maritime History are directed to the office of Professor Halvard Rennick on the second floor of the humanities building. As head of department he oversees the teaching programme, the oral history interviews and the care of the department's collection of maritime maps.

Pellam Observatory was designed by the architect Edmund Fairclough, who planned the stone tower and its telescope dome for Asterford University. Fairclough insisted on thick foundations so that the instruments would stay steady in strong winds, and he included a small reading room at the base of the tower for visiting astronomers.

The architect Edmund Fairclough is remembered in Asterford mainly as the designer of Pellam Observatory on the hill above the campus. His drawings for the observatory, which show the dome, the spiral staircase and the lecture room, are kept by the university and are sometimes displayed during open days.

Visitors often ask who designed Pellam Observatory, and the answer given on the plaque by the entrance is Edmund Fairclough. He combined careful decoration with practical engineering, placing the telescope on a heavy tower and adding wide windows so that the lecture room below would be bright during the day.

Professor Orla Penhaligon teaches volcanology at Asterford University. Her lectures explain how volcanoes form, erupt and change the land around them, and she often brings rock samples from her field work into the classroom so that students can handle cooled lava and ash for themselves. Her course is popular in Earth Sciences.

The subject taught by Professor Orla Penhaligon is volcanology, and her course in the Department of Earth Sciences covers eruptions, lava flows and the monitoring of active volcanoes. Each spring she leads a field trip so that students can study volcanic rock formations and learn how scientists measure ground movement.

Professor Orla Penhaligon is a volcanology lecturer at Asterford University and teaches the subject to second and third year students. In her classes students build simple models of eruptions, read records of historic volcanic events and discuss how towns near active volcanoes prepare for emergencies.

Professor Orla Penhaligon won the Harrowgate Prize for her field research in cold northern regions. The prize is awarded every three years to a scientist whose work has made an outstanding contribution to earth sciences, and she was the first member of Asterford University staff to receive it.

The Harrowgate Prize was presented to Professor Orla Penhaligon at a ceremony attended by colleagues from across Asterford University. The award recognised her long programme of field work and her clear teaching, and the prize certificate is now displayed in a glass case in the Department of Earth Sciences.

Among the honours received by Professor Orla Penhaligon, the most important is the Harrowgate Prize, which she won for research that changed how scientists study the far north. The university marked the award with a public lecture in which she described her expeditions and the instruments her team used.

Kestrel Boathouse, the home of the Asterford University Boat Club, is built from pine. The timber was chosen because it was light, cheap and easy to work, and the pale walls of the boathouse are a familiar sight for walkers and joggers on the towpath beside the River Wend.

The material used to build Kestrel Boathouse is pine, cut from forests in the hills north of Asterford. Local carpenters assembled the frame in a single summer, and the boat club still treats the pine boards every autumn with oil so that they survive the damp air beside the river.

Kestrel Boathouse is a pine building on the bank of the River Wend, used by the Asterford University Boat Club for storing boats and holding training sessions. Its pine walls and roof beams were restored ten years ago, when the club also added a small changing room and a first aid station.

On weekdays the Campus Loop shuttle runs every 30 minutes, linking the teaching buildings of Asterford University with the residences and the town centre. Because the service is not frequent, students are advised to check the timetable posted at each stop and to allow extra time when travelling to morning lectures.

The Campus Loop shuttle operates every 30 minutes on weekdays, according to the timetable published by the university transport office. This pattern was introduced to save energy and reduce traffic on Mill Road, and the electric buses wait at each main stop for a few minutes before continuing.

Students often ask how often the Campus Loop shuttle runs on weekdays, and the transport office answers that a bus leaves every 30 minutes. At weekends the timetable changes, but from Monday to Friday the same pattern is kept from early morning until the last service in the evening.

The Campus Loop shuttle starts at Corbel Square, the paved square in front of the Asterford town hall. From the square the electric buses travel past the Student Union, the science buildings and the residences before returning, so students living in the old town can reach the campus without a long walk.

Corbel Square is the starting point of the Campus Loop shuttle, and the first bus of the day leaves the square shortly after seven in the morning. A small shelter with a printed map of the route stands at the corner of the square, next to a bakery that is popular with early passengers.

Passengers who ask where the Campus Loop shuttle starts are directed to Corbel Square in the centre of Asterford. The square was chosen as the first stop because many buses from nearby villages also stop there, making it easy for commuting students to change onto the shuttle.

Students who work in the Sable Chemistry Laboratory are required to wear violet lab coats. This colour was adopted so that teaching staff can easily separate students from the technicians, and so that a student who walks out of the laboratory still dressed in a coat is spotted straight away at the exit.

The lab coats worn by students in the Sable Chemistry Laboratory are violet, a colour chosen by the head of the laboratory when new safety rules were introduced. Each student receives two violet coats at the start of the year and must return them for cleaning at the end of every term.

Visitors to the Sable Chemistry Laboratory notice at once that the students wear violet lab coats while the technicians wear grey. The violet coats are made from a fire-resistant fabric and carry a small badge with the student's name, which helps teachers during busy practical classes.

The Winter Book Fair of Asterford University is held in Ashcombe Hall, a large stone hall that is normally used for concerts and graduation ceremonies. During the fair the long tables of Ashcombe Hall are covered with second-hand books, rare editions and old maps, and the gallery becomes a quiet reading area.

Ashcombe Hall hosts the Winter Book Fair every year, when booksellers from across the region set up their stalls beneath its high painted ceiling. The hall is close to the main gate, so visitors from the town can easily find the fair, and volunteers serve hot drinks at the entrance.

Visitors who ask which hall hosts the Winter Book Fair are sent to Ashcombe Hall on the north side of the quadrangle. The hall has hosted the fair since it was first organised, and its size allows more than sixty booksellers to display their stock at the same time.

The Winter Book Fair runs for six days and draws book lovers from all over the region to Asterford. Every day of the fair follows a different theme, for example poetry, travel writing or children's books, and visiting authors give readings each evening in the main hall.

Organisers of the Winter Book Fair at Asterford University plan the event to last six days, opening on a Monday and closing on the Saturday evening. The longer programme gives booksellers time to sell their stock and allows students to visit the fair between lectures during the week.

People often ask how long the Winter Book Fair lasts, and the answer printed in the official programme is six days. During that time the fair hosts book sales, author talks and a special auction of rare maps, with the proceeds going to the university library fund.
